stimuli.title: Reading comprehension
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

In many villages of India, the clatter of the handloom was once heard from morning till night. A skilled weaver could spend a week on a single sari, and the cloth carried patterns handed down through families for generations. Over the last fifty years, however, cheap cloth from power looms has taken much of this market. A power-loom sari that looks similar at a glance can be sold at a fraction of the price, and many buyers do not know, or do not care, how their cloth was made. Young people in weaving families have drifted to factory and city jobs that pay a steady wage.

The weaver's problem is often not skill but access. Most weavers sell to a local trader who supplies the yarn, buys the finished cloth and sets the price. The trader carries the risk of unsold stock, so he pays little, and the weaver rarely learns what the cloth finally sells for in a city shop.

Online selling has begun to open a second door. A cooperative that photographs its saris and lists them on a website or a social media page can reach buyers in distant cities who are willing to pay more for genuine handwoven cloth. Some groups now attach a short note to each piece naming the weaver and the number of days it took to make. Buyers say this story is part of what they pay for.

The new door has its own costs. Good photographs, careful packing, returns and online payments all demand skills that weavers did not need before. Cooperatives that have succeeded usually had help, from a designer who suggested colours that city buyers want or a young member who managed the website.

Handloom will not win a price war against the power loom, and it does not need to. Its future lies with buyers who value what only a pair of hands and a wooden loom can make, and with finding ways to reach those buyers directly.

stimuli.title: Reading comprehension
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A few years ago, a vegetable seller on a city pavement dealt only in cash. Customers who forgot their wallets walked away, and at the end of each day the seller counted a bag of coins and crumpled notes, part of which went to a moneylender who had advanced the morning's stock at a steep daily rate. Today many such sellers display a printed QR code on a piece of cardboard beside their scales. A customer scans it with a phone, and the payment reaches the seller's bank account within seconds.

The change has brought more than convenience. Because each payment is recorded, the seller's account now shows a history of daily sales. Banks that once had no way to judge a street vendor's income can look at these records and offer a small working-capital loan at a far lower rate than the moneylender's. For many vendors, this is the first loan they have ever received from a bank.

The shift is not complete. Some older vendors distrust payments they cannot hold in their hands, and a few have lost money to fraudsters who send fake payment messages or ask them to scan a code to 'receive' money. Network failures in crowded markets can also leave a customer and a seller staring at a screen that will not load. For these reasons, most vendors still keep a cash box alongside the QR code.

Experts argue that the next step is not more technology but more trust. Simple training in spotting fraud, quick help when a payment goes astray and patient explanation by bank staff in the local language would do more than any new app to bring the remaining vendors on board.

The cardboard QR code may look humble, but for many small sellers it has become a bridge between the pavement and the formal banking system.

stimuli.title: Short passage
stimuli.text:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Young people who take up their first job often find that their salary disappears faster than they expected. Rent, travel and food take the first share, and small online purchases quietly take the rest. Advisers suggest a habit that sounds old-fashioned but works: on the day the salary arrives, move a fixed part of it into a separate savings account or a recurring deposit before spending anything. Saving what is left at the end of the month rarely works, because little is ever left. The fixed amount can be small at first; what matters is that it is set aside first and without fail. Over time the habit, more than the amount, builds a cushion for emergencies.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Young people should be kept from leaving weaving families
Weavers have lost their skills over the last fifty years
Local traders pay weavers more than city shops ever could
Handloom can last by reaching buyers who value handwoven cloth
Power looms should be banned to protect handloom weavers
questions.explanation: The passage explains why handloom lost its market and ends by saying its future lies with 'buyers who value what only a pair of hands and a wooden loom can make' and reaching them directly. It says the problem is access, not skill, and never calls for a ban.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why has handloom lost much of its market?
options: Similar-looking power-loom cloth sells far more cheaply
Handwoven saris are no longer allowed in city shops
Buyers now prefer plain cloth without any pattern
The government has stopped buying handwoven cloth
Weavers have run short of yarn in recent years
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says 'a power-loom sari that looks similar at a glance can be sold at a fraction of the price'.

questions.stem: What does the local trader do, according to the passage?
options: Lends weavers money to buy power looms
Supplies yarn, buys the cloth and sets the price
Teaches young weavers the family patterns
Sells the weavers' saris on a website
Photographs each sari for city buyers
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the trader 'supplies the yarn, buys the finished cloth and sets the price'.

questions.stem: Why, according to the passage, does the trader pay the weaver little?
options: He sells the cloth abroad at a lower price
He must pay a designer to choose new colours
He is required by law to keep prices low
He knows the weaver will soon leave for the city
He bears the risk that some cloth will not sell
questions.explanation: The passage says 'the trader carries the risk of unsold stock, so he pays little'.

questions.stem: What do some cooperatives now attach to each piece of cloth?
options: A certificate from a government textile office
A note naming the weaver and the days it took
A sample of the yarn used to weave the sari
A discount coupon for the buyer's next purchase
A photograph of the city shop that sells it
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says some groups attach 'a short note to each piece naming the weaver and the number of days it took to make'.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as something online selling demands?
options: Renting a showroom in a big city
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph lists 'good photographs, careful packing, returns and online payments'. A city showroom is never mentioned.

questions.stem: What does the writer mean by saying handloom 'will not win a price war against the power loom, and it does not need to'?
options: Its buyers pay for craft and story, not for the lowest price
City buyers no longer compare the prices of saris
Handloom saris already cost less than power-loom saris
Weavers should cut their prices until they match factories
Power looms will soon stop making saris altogether
questions.explanation: The next sentence says handloom's future lies with buyers who value handmade cloth. It need not be cheapest because those buyers pay for what a hand loom makes and the story behind it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the tone of the passage?
questions.explanation: The writer is frank about the costs and the lost market but sees a real way forward: realistic but hopeful.

questions.stem: Choose the word most similar in meaning to 'drifted' as used in the passage.
questions.explanation: Young people 'have drifted to factory and city jobs' means they have gradually moved there. 'Floated' is the literal sense of drift, not the one used here.

questions.stem: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'genuine' as used in the passage.
questions.explanation: 'Genuine handwoven cloth' means real, authentic cloth. The opposite is 'fake'; the other options are close in meaning to 'genuine'.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (1) best?
questions.explanation: At first the members are unsure, so they 'may wonder whether' small savings help. 'Insist whether' and 'promise whether' are not idiomatic, and the next sentence ('however') shows doubt, not certainty.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (2) best?
questions.explanation: Because every member knows the borrower, repayment is usually high. 'Rarely', 'never', 'hardly' and 'seldom' would contradict the reason given.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (3) best?
questions.explanation: Proper records give a bank confidence, so it is 'willing to lend'. 'Afraid', 'unable', 'forbidden' and 'reluctant' all reverse the sense of 'once the group has kept proper records'.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (4) best?
questions.explanation: What members gain 'from speaking at meetings and dealing with officials' is confidence. The sentence contrasts it with money, so 'salary' and 'property' do not fit.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (5) best?
questions.explanation: The group 'gives its members a voice as well as a purse', summing up the two gains in the passage. 'Takes', 'costs' and 'denies' reverse the meaning.

questions.stem:

questions.stem:

The box was **too heavy that he could not** lift it.

too heavy so that he could not
very heavy that he could not
heavy enough that he could not
questions.explanation: The pattern is 'so ... that': 'so heavy that he could not lift it'. 'Too' is used with 'to': 'too heavy to lift'.

questions.stem: What amount will ₹16,000 grow to in 2 years at 10% per annum, compounded annually?
questions.explanation: After year 1: 16,000 × 1.1 = 17,600. After year 2: 17,600 × 1.1 = ₹19,360. (₹19,200 would be simple interest.)

questions.stem: The average age of 30 students in a class is 14 years. When the teacher's age is included, the average rises by 1 year. What is the teacher's age?
questions.explanation: The 31 people now average 15 years, a total of 465. The students alone total 30 × 14 = 420. The teacher is 465 − 420 = 45.

questions.stem: Anita and Bhavesh start a business with ₹24,000 and ₹36,000 for one year. Out of a profit of ₹15,000, what is Anita's share?
questions.explanation: Shares are in the ratio 24,000 : 36,000 = 2 : 3. Anita gets 2/5 of 15,000 = ₹6,000.

questions.stem: Pipe A can fill a tank in 6 hours and pipe B can empty the full tank in 18 hours. If both are opened together on an empty tank, in how many hours will it be full?
questions.explanation: Each hour the tank gains 1/6 − 1/18 = 3/18 − 1/18 = 2/18 = 1/9, so it fills in 9 hours. (4.5 hours would come from adding the two rates, as if B also filled the tank.)

questions.stem: Walking at 4 km/h, Harish reaches his office 12 minutes late. Walking at 5 km/h, he reaches 9 minutes early. How far is his office?
questions.explanation: The two times differ by 21 minutes, or 21/60 hour. d/4 − d/5 = d/20, so d/20 = 21/60 and d = 7 km.

questions.stem: A candidate needs 40% of the maximum marks to pass. Sunita scored 186 marks and failed by 34 marks. What are the maximum marks?
questions.explanation: The pass mark is 186 + 34 = 220, which is 40% of the maximum. 220 ÷ 0.4 = 550.

questions.stem: The sum of the present ages of a father and his son is 50 years. Five years ago, the father was four times as old as the son. What is the son's present age?
questions.explanation: Let the son be S, so the father is 50 − S. Five years ago: 45 − S = 4(S − 5), so 45 − S = 4S − 20, 5S = 65 and S = 13. (The father is 37; five years ago 32 = 4 × 8.)

questions.stem: A bag has 3 red, 6 blue and 5 green balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is NOT blue?
questions.explanation: There are 14 balls and 8 of them are not blue, so the probability is 8/14 = 4/7.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: M ≥ N > O = P < Q

I. M > P

II. Q > O
questions.explanation: I: M ≥ N > O = P gives M > P, true. II: Q > P = O gives Q > O, true. Both follow.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: F > G ≥ H < J = K

I. F > H

II. G < K
questions.explanation: I: F > G ≥ H gives F > H, true. II: G ≥ H and H < J point in opposite directions, so G and K cannot be compared. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: G ≤ H < I ≥ J > K

I. H > K

II. I > K
questions.explanation: I: H < I and I ≥ J point in opposite directions, so H and K cannot be compared. II: I ≥ J > K gives I > K, true. Only II follows.

questions.stem:
A statement is followed by two conclusions, I and II. Assume the statement is true and decide which conclusion(s) definitely follow.

Statement: J ≤ K = L ≤ M > N

I. M > J

II. M = J
questions.explanation: J ≤ K = L ≤ M gives M ≥ J. Neither 'M > J' nor 'M = J' is certain alone, but one of them must be true. Either I or II follows.

questions.stem:

questions.explanation: Nothing says every toy is a gift, so I is not certain. The gifts that are kites are also toys, so some toys are gifts (II). Only II follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: All shops are stalls. Some shops are kiosks.

I. Some stalls are kiosks.

II. All kiosks are stalls.
questions.explanation: The shops that are kiosks are also stalls, so some stalls are kiosks (I). The kiosks that are not shops may or may not be stalls, so II is not certain. Only I follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: No pot is a pan. Some pans are jugs.

I. Some jugs are pots.

II. No jug is a pot.
questions.explanation: Jugs that are not pans may or may not be pots, so neither conclusion is certain alone. But they cover every case between them (either some jugs are pots or none is), so either I or II follows.

questions.stem:
Some statements are followed by two conclusions, I and II. Take the statements to be true even if they seem to differ from commonly known facts, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow.

Statements: No sock is a shoe. All boots are shoes.

I. No boot is a sock.

II. Some shoes are not socks.
questions.explanation: Every boot is a shoe and no shoe is a sock, so no boot is a sock (I). The shoes that are boots are not socks, so some shoes are not socks (II). Both follow.

questions.stem: Who sits at the extreme left end of the row?
questions.explanation: Left to right: L, P, J, N, K, O, M. N is 4th (the middle of seven), M is three places to its right (7th), K is 5th and J, second to the left of K, is 3rd. O is immediately left of M (6th). L and P take 1st and 2nd, and P is not at an end, so P is 2nd and L 1st.

questions.stem: How many persons sit between P and K?
questions.explanation: Left to right: L, P, J, N, K, O, M. N is 4th (the middle of seven), M is three places to its right (7th), K is 5th and J, second to the left of K, is 3rd. O is immediately left of M (6th). L and P take 1st and 2nd, and P is not at an end, so P is 2nd and L 1st. P is 2nd and K 5th, so J and N sit between them.

questions.stem: Who sits second to the right of J?
questions.explanation: Left to right: L, P, J, N, K, O, M. N is 4th (the middle of seven), M is three places to its right (7th), K is 5th and J, second to the left of K, is 3rd. O is immediately left of M (6th). L and P take 1st and 2nd, and P is not at an end, so P is 2nd and L 1st. J is 3rd; second to the right is 5th, K.

questions.stem: Which pair sits at the two ends of the row?
questions.explanation: Left to right: L, P, J, N, K, O, M. N is 4th (the middle of seven), M is three places to its right (7th), K is 5th and J, second to the left of K, is 3rd. O is immediately left of M (6th). L and P take 1st and 2nd, and P is not at an end, so P is 2nd and L 1st.

questions.stem: What is O's position counted from the right end of the row?
questions.explanation: Left to right: L, P, J, N, K, O, M. N is 4th (the middle of seven), M is three places to its right (7th), K is 5th and J, second to the left of K, is 3rd. O is immediately left of M (6th). L and P take 1st and 2nd, and P is not at an end, so P is 2nd and L 1st. O is 6th from the left of seven, so 2nd from the right.

questions.stem: In which month does Rohan take his exam?
questions.explanation: In order: January Meera, March Rohan, April Kavya, July Nitin, September Pallavi, November Lokesh. Lokesh has November, the last month. With one person between them, Nitin has July, and Kavya the month before, April. Of January, March and September, only September has 30 days, so Pallavi has September. Meera comes before Rohan: Meera January, Rohan March.

questions.stem: Who takes the exam in January?
questions.explanation: In order: January Meera, March Rohan, April Kavya, July Nitin, September Pallavi, November Lokesh. Lokesh has November, the last month. With one person between them, Nitin has July, and Kavya the month before, April. Of January, March and September, only September has 30 days, so Pallavi has September. Meera comes before Rohan: Meera January, Rohan March.

questions.stem: How many persons take their exams between Meera and Kavya?
questions.explanation: In order: January Meera, March Rohan, April Kavya, July Nitin, September Pallavi, November Lokesh. Lokesh has November, the last month. With one person between them, Nitin has July, and Kavya the month before, April. Of January, March and September, only September has 30 days, so Pallavi has September. Meera comes before Rohan: Meera January, Rohan March. Only Rohan (March) falls between Meera (January) and Kavya (April).

questions.stem: Whose exam comes immediately after Kavya's?
questions.explanation: In order: January Meera, March Rohan, April Kavya, July Nitin, September Pallavi, November Lokesh. Lokesh has November, the last month. With one person between them, Nitin has July, and Kavya the month before, April. Of January, March and September, only September has 30 days, so Pallavi has September. Meera comes before Rohan: Meera January, Rohan March.

questions.explanation: In order: January Meera, March Rohan, April Kavya, July Nitin, September Pallavi, November Lokesh. Lokesh has November, the last month. questions.stem: Who sits opposite T?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): P, T, R, V, Q, W, S, U. Clockwise from S come U and then P. R is three seats anticlockwise of W, and T three seats anticlockwise of Q, so W and Q take the two seats just anticlockwise of S, R and T the two seats just clockwise of P, and V the seat between those pairs. V is next to R, so R sits beside V and T beside P; then Q sits beside V and W beside S. T is the seat immediately clockwise of P; four seats on from T is W.

questions.stem: Who sits immediately to the right of Q?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): P, T, R, V, Q, W, S, U. Clockwise from S come U and then P. R is three seats anticlockwise of W, and T three seats anticlockwise of Q, so W and Q take the two seats just anticlockwise of S, R and T the two seats just clockwise of P, and V the seat between those pairs. V is next to R, so R sits beside V and T beside P; then Q sits beside V and W beside S. A person's right is the next seat anticlockwise, so Q's immediate right is V. W is on Q's left.

questions.stem: How many persons sit between U and R, counting clockwise from U?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): P, T, R, V, Q, W, S, U. Clockwise from S come U and then P. R is three seats anticlockwise of W, and T three seats anticlockwise of Q, so W and Q take the two seats just anticlockwise of S, R and T the two seats just clockwise of P, and V the seat between those pairs. V is next to R, so R sits beside V and T beside P; then Q sits beside V and W beside S. Clockwise from U come P and T, then R.

questions.stem: Who sits third to the left of W?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): P, T, R, V, Q, W, S, U. Clockwise from S come U and then P. R is three seats anticlockwise of W, and T three seats anticlockwise of Q, so W and Q take the two seats just anticlockwise of S, R and T the two seats just clockwise of P, and V the seat between those pairs. V is next to R, so R sits beside V and T beside P; then Q sits beside V and W beside S. Moving clockwise (left) from W: S, U, then P.

questions.stem: Which pair sits opposite each other?
questions.explanation: Clockwise from P (facing the centre, a person's left is the next seat clockwise): P, T, R, V, Q, W, S, U. Clockwise from S come U and then P. R is three seats anticlockwise of W, and T three seats anticlockwise of Q, so W and Q take the two seats just anticlockwise of S, R and T the two seats just clockwise of P, and V the seat between those pairs. V is next to R, so R sits beside V and T beside P; then Q sits beside V and W beside S.

questions.stem: In a certain code, CASH is written as DBTI. How is NOTE written in that code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves one place forward: C→D, A→B, S→T, H→I. So N→O, O→P, T→U, E→F: OPUF.

questions.stem: In a certain code, BANK is written as LOBC. How is FUND written in that code?
questions.explanation: The word is reversed and each letter moved one place forward: BANK → KNAB → LOBC. FUND → DNUF → EOVG.

questions.stem: In a certain code language, 'pay bill now' is written as 'ko ru ta', 'bill is due' as 'ta mi le' and 'now or later' as 'ru si vo'. What is the code for 'pay'?
questions.explanation: 'Bill' appears in the first two sentences, and so does 'ta'. 'Now' appears in the first and third, and so does 'ru'. The code left for 'pay' is 'ko'.

questions.stem: Pointing to a girl, Ramesh says, "Her mother is the only sister of my wife." How is the girl related to Ramesh?
questions.explanation: The girl's mother is Ramesh's wife's sister, his sister-in-law. Her daughter is Ramesh's niece.

questions.stem: A is the brother of B. C is the mother of A. D is the father of C. How is B related to D?
questions.explanation: B is a child of C (A's brother's sibling shares the mother C), and C is D's daughter, so B is D's grandchild. B's gender is not given, so neither 'grandson' nor 'granddaughter' is certain.

questions.stem: Nikhil walks 6 km north, turns right and walks 8 km, then turns right again and walks 6 km. How far is he from his starting point, and in which direction?
questions.explanation: After 6 km north and 8 km east, turning right faces him south. 6 km south brings him back level with the start, 8 km to its east.

questions.stem: Farhan is facing south. He turns 135° clockwise and then 45° anticlockwise. Which direction is he facing now?
questions.explanation: From south, 90° clockwise is west and 135° is north-west. Turning back 45° anticlockwise leaves him facing west.

questions.stem: In a row of 61 students, Payal is 23rd from the left end. What is her position from the right end?
questions.explanation: Position from the right = total − position from the left + 1 = 61 − 23 + 1 = 39th.

questions.stem: Which letter is 7th to the right of the 15th letter from the left in the English alphabet?
questions.explanation: The 15th letter is O. Seven places to its right is the 22nd letter, V.

questions.stem: Which letter pair comes next in the series? AY, BX, CW, DV, ?
questions.explanation: The first letters move forward (A, B, C, D, E) and the second letters move backward (Y, X, W, V, U): EU.

questions.stem: If the letters of the word MARKET are arranged in alphabetical order, which letter will be third from the right?
questions.explanation: In alphabetical order the letters are A, E, K, M, R, T. Third from the right is M.

questions.stem: Find the odd one out: 64, 100, 144, 160, 196
questions.explanation: 64, 100, 144 and 196 are the squares of 8, 10, 12 and 14. 160 is not a perfect square.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the passage?
options: How to Build a Mobile Payment App
The Rising Price of City Vegetables
Street Vendors and the Road to the Bank
questions.explanation: The passage is about how QR payments are linking street vendors to banks and what still holds some back. The other titles pick up a single detail or are not discussed.

questions.stem: How did the vegetable seller pay for the morning's stock before digital payments?
options: With credit from the wholesale market
With a loan from the nearest bank
With an advance from a moneylender
With savings kept in a post office
With money sent by city relatives
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says part of the day's cash went to 'a moneylender who had advanced the morning's stock at a steep daily rate'.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how do QR payments help a vendor get a bank loan?
options: The moneylender passes the vendor's records to the bank
The recorded payments show the bank a history of sales
Customers guarantee the loan when they scan the code
The payment app lends money to the vendor directly
The bank gives a loan to everyone who displays a code
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says 'each payment is recorded', so the account shows 'a history of daily sales' that banks can use to judge income.

questions.stem: Why do most vendors still keep a cash box?
options: The QR code must be replaced by a new one every day
Banks do not allow vendors to receive large payments
Customers are not allowed to pay small sums by phone
Moneylenders insist on being repaid only in cash
Distrust, fraud and network failures make cash a backup
questions.explanation: The third paragraph lists older vendors' distrust, fraudsters and network failures, then says 'for these reasons, most vendors still keep a cash box'.

questions.stem: Which trick used by fraudsters is described in the passage?
options: Paying with notes that turn out to be counterfeit
Stealing the vendor's phone at the end of the day
Asking the vendor to scan a code to 'receive' money
Changing the vendor's printed code at night
Posing as bank staff offering cheap loans
questions.explanation: The passage mentions 'fake payment messages' and asking vendors 'to scan a code to receive money'.

questions.stem: What do experts say would bring the remaining vendors on board?
options: A new app that works without any internet connection
A law requiring every customer to pay by phone
Closing the cash counters at local banks
Training, quick help and explanation in the local language
Higher loans for vendors who give up cash
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says training in spotting fraud, quick help and patient explanation in the local language 'would do more than any new app'.

questions.stem: What does the writer mean by calling the QR code 'a bridge between the pavement and the formal banking system'?
options: It replaces bank branches in crowded city markets
It lets vendors move their stalls into bank buildings
It is a path that customers use to cross the road
It allows banks to collect rent from pavement sellers
It links small sellers to banks and their services
questions.explanation: Through QR payments vendors gain bank accounts, records and loans: the code connects street trade with formal banking.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as a problem with QR payments?
options: Requests to scan a fake code
A fee charged on every payment
questions.explanation: The passage mentions distrust, fake messages, scam codes and network failures, but never any fee on payments.

questions.stem: Choose the word most similar in meaning to 'steep' as used in the passage.
questions.explanation: A 'steep daily rate' is a very high, excessive rate of interest. 'Sloping' is the literal meaning of steep, not the one used here.

questions.stem: Choose the word most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to 'humble' as used in the passage.
questions.explanation: The cardboard code 'may look humble', that is, simple and modest. The opposite is 'grand'.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (1) best?
questions.explanation: 'This trust is often justified, but not always' means it is usually deserved. The phrase 'but not always' needs a word that is mostly true; the other options are negative.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (2) best?
questions.explanation: The charges are not hidden 'since each is mentioned somewhere in the document'. 'Removed' or 'forgotten' would mean they are not in the document at all.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (3) best?
questions.explanation: Counsellors recommend a simple habit, which the sentence then describes. 'Prohibit' and 'regret' reverse the sense.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (4) best?
questions.explanation: The total repayment captures, or includes, the costs spread across the pages. 'Hides' and 'excludes' say the opposite, and the figure cannot cancel or double costs.

questions.stem: Which word fits blank (5) best?
questions.explanation: A borrower who knows the total cost is less likely to be surprised later by extra charges. The other words do not fit an unpleasant discovery.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

Please ........ the form in capital letters and sign it at the bottom.
questions.explanation: A form is filled in (or filled out). The other prepositions are not used with 'form'.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

The customer was ........ about the extra charge and asked for a written explanation.
questions.explanation: Someone who asks for an explanation of a charge is puzzled by it. 'Fond about' and 'proud about' are unidiomatic, and 'pleased' does not fit the request.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

The two branches will be ........ next month to cut running costs.
questions.explanation: Branches, banks and companies are 'merged'. 'Mixed' and 'melted' are used for substances, and 'joined up' is informal and unusual here.

questions.stem:
Choose the pair of words that fits the two blanks, in order, to make the sentence meaningful.

The road was ........ for repairs, so the buses had to take a ........ route.
questions.explanation: A road closed for repairs forces buses onto a longer route. 'Opened, shorter' and 'closed, faster' do not follow, and the last two pairs make no sense in the second blank.

questions.stem:
Choose the pair of words that fits the two blanks, in order, to make the sentence meaningful.

Although the task looked ........ at first, it turned out to be quite .........
questions.explanation: 'Although' needs a contrast: difficult at first, but simple in the end. Every other pair has two words with the same meaning.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

A pair of shoes (A) / are kept (B) / near the door (C) / for guests. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: The subject is 'a pair', which is singular: 'A pair of shoes is kept near the door'.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

Being a public holiday, (A) / the bank (B) / remained closed (C) / all day. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: As written, 'being a public holiday' describes 'the bank', which makes no sense. The opening needs its own subject: 'It being a public holiday, the bank remained closed' (or 'As it was a public holiday, ...').

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

Who's pen (A) / is this (B) / lying on (C) / the counter? (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Who's' is short for 'who is'. The possessive is 'whose': 'Whose pen is this lying on the counter?'

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

The scissors (A) / is kept (B) / in the top drawer (C) / of the desk. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Scissors' is a plural noun (like 'trousers' and 'spectacles'), so it takes 'are': 'The scissors are kept ...'. ('A pair of scissors is' would be singular.)

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

The officer asked (A) / the visitor to wait (B) / outside the cabin (C) / for a few minutes. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: The sentence is correct: 'asked someone to wait' is the right pattern, and the rest of the sentence agrees.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

If I **was the manager**, I would open the branch on Sundays.
questions.explanation: An imaginary present condition uses 'were' for every subject: 'If I were the manager, I would ...'.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

He **has been working** in this bank for twelve years.
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous with 'for twelve years' is correct for an action that began in the past and is still going on.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

The manager made him **to wait** outside the cabin for an hour.
questions.explanation: 'Make' in the active voice takes the bare infinitive without 'to': 'made him wait'. ('He was made to wait' keeps 'to' only in the passive.)

questions.stem:
The parts of a sentence, labelled P, Q, R and S, are given in jumbled order after the fixed opening. Choose the order that makes a meaningful sentence.

To open a savings account,

P. along with two photographs
Q. you must fill in the form
R. and submit it at the counter
S. and a copy of your identity proof
questions.explanation: To open a savings account, (Q) you must fill in the form (P) along with two photographs (S) and a copy of your identity proof (R) and submit it at the counter.

questions.stem:
The parts of a sentence, labelled P, Q, R and S, are given in jumbled order after the fixed opening. Choose the order that makes a meaningful sentence.

The farmers of the village

P. where they could sell
Q. formed a cooperative
R. their milk directly
S. and set up a collection centre
questions.explanation: The farmers of the village (Q) formed a cooperative (S) and set up a collection centre (P) where they could sell (R) their milk directly.

questions.stem: How many passengers used route R3 over the three days together?
questions.explanation: 62 + 55 + 58 = 175 hundred, which is 17,500 passengers.

questions.stem: What was the average number of passengers per route on Wednesday?
questions.explanation: Wednesday total = 60 + 47 + 58 + 45 = 210 hundred. 210 ÷ 4 = 52.5 hundred, which is 5,250.

questions.stem: By what percentage did the passengers on route R4 rise from Monday to Wednesday?
questions.explanation: R4 rose from 30 to 45 hundred, an increase of 15. 15 ÷ 30 × 100 = 50%.

questions.stem: What is the ratio of passengers on route R2 to passengers on route R1, both on Monday?
questions.explanation: R2 on Monday had 36 and R1 had 45. 36 : 45, dividing both by 9, is 4 : 5.

questions.stem: By how many passengers did route R3 on Monday exceed route R2 on Tuesday?
questions.explanation: R3 on Monday had 62 hundred and R2 on Tuesday 40 hundred. 62 − 40 = 22 hundred, which is 2,200.

questions.stem: Whose savings are the largest percentage of their income?
questions.explanation: Savings as a share of income: Ravi 12/48 = 25%, Seema 18/60 = 30%, Tanvir 11/55 = 20%, Usha 14/40 = 35%, Vijay 18/72 = 25%. Usha is highest.

questions.stem: What are the total monthly savings of all five persons?
questions.explanation: Savings are 12, 18, 11, 14 and 18 thousand, which add to 73 thousand: ₹73,000.

questions.stem: Tanvir's expenditure is what percentage of his income?
What is the average monthly income of the five persons?
What is the ratio of Seema's savings to Usha's savings?
questions.explanation: Seema saves 60 − 42 = 18 thousand and Usha 40 − 26 = 14 thousand. 18 : 14 = 9 : 7.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper marks an article 25% above its cost price and then gives a discount of 8%. What is his profit percentage?
questions.explanation: If the cost is 100, the marked price is 125 and the selling price is 92% of 125 = 115. Profit = 15%.

questions.stem: ₹4,500 earns ₹810 as simple interest in 2 years. What is the rate of interest per annum?
What is the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on ₹18,000 for 2 years at 5% per annum, compounded annually?
questions.explanation: For 2 years the difference is P × (R/100)² = 18,000 × 0.05 × 0.05 = ₹45.

questions.stem: The average of six numbers is 28. If one of them, 38, is replaced by 20, what is the new average?
questions.explanation: The total falls from 6 × 28 = 168 by 18 to 150, and 150 ÷ 6 = 25.

questions.stem: An 80-litre mixture has milk and water in the ratio 5 : 3. How many litres of water must be added to make the ratio 5 : 4?
questions.explanation: Milk = 50 litres and water = 30 litres. For 5 : 4, water must be 50 ÷ 5 × 4 = 40 litres, so add 10.

questions.stem: Kiran and Lata together can finish a piece of work in 12 days. Kiran alone can finish it in 20 days. In how many days can Lata finish it alone?
questions.explanation: Lata's daily work = 1/12 − 1/20 = 5/60 − 3/60 = 2/60 = 1/30, so she needs 30 days.

questions.stem: A boat's speed in still water is 18 km/h and the stream flows at 6 km/h. How long will the boat take to go 72 km downstream and come back?
questions.explanation: Downstream speed is 24 km/h (3 hours for 72 km); upstream speed is 12 km/h (6 hours). Total 9 hours.

questions.stem: A town has 25,000 people. Its population rises by 8% in one year and falls by 5% the next. What is the population after two years?
The incomes of Mohit and Naina are in the ratio 5 : 4 and their expenditures in the ratio 3 : 2. If each saves ₹6,000 a month, what is Mohit's income?
questions.explanation: Let incomes be 5k and 4k and expenditures 3m and 2m. 5k − 3m = 6,000 and 4k − 2m = 6,000 give m = 2k − 3,000, so 5k − 6k + 9,000 = 6,000 and k = 3,000. Mohit earns 5 × 3,000 = ₹15,000.

questions.stem: Two trains 175 m and 225 m long run on parallel tracks in opposite directions at 48 km/h and 72 km/h. How long do they take to cross each other completely?
questions.explanation: Relative speed = 48 + 72 = 120 km/h = 100/3 m/s. They must cover 175 + 225 = 400 m, which takes 400 × 3/100 = 12 seconds.

questions.stem:

I. P > S

II. R ≥ P
questions.explanation: I: P > Q ≥ R > S gives P > S, true. II: P > Q ≥ R gives P > R, so 'R ≥ P' is false. Only I follows.

questions.stem:

I. W > Z

questions.explanation: X ≥ Y and Y ≤ Z point in opposite directions, so neither W nor X can be compared with Z. Neither follows.

I. D > F

questions.explanation: D ≥ E ≥ F gives D ≥ F. Neither 'D > F' nor 'D = F' is certain alone, but one must be true. Either I or II follows.

questions.stem:

questions.stem: Who attends on Wednesday?
questions.explanation: Monday to Sunday: F, C, H, B, E, G, D. B is on Thursday, so D, three days later, is on Sunday. E is on Friday and G on Saturday. F, C and H take Monday to Wednesday in that order.

questions.stem: How many persons attend between F and E?
questions.explanation: Monday to Sunday: F, C, H, B, E, G, D. B is on Thursday, so D, three days later, is on Sunday. E is on Friday and G on Saturday. F, C and H take Monday to Wednesday in that order. C, H and B attend between Monday (F) and Friday (E).

questions.stem: On which day does C attend?
questions.explanation: Monday to Sunday: F, C, H, B, E, G, D. B is on Thursday, so D, three days later, is on Sunday. E is on Friday and G on Saturday. F, C and H take Monday to Wednesday in that order.

questions.stem: Who attends on the day immediately after G?
questions.explanation: Monday to Sunday: F, C, H, B, E, G, D. B is on Thursday, so D, three days later, is on Sunday. E is on Friday and G on Saturday. F, C and H take Monday to Wednesday in that order.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: Monday to Sunday: F, C, H, B, E, G, D. B is on Thursday, so D, three days later, is on Sunday. E is on Friday and G on Saturday. F, C and H take Monday to Wednesday in that order.

questions.stem: Who has the most books?
questions.explanation: Most to fewest: C, A, F, D, B, E. C > A > F > D, B has more than only E, so B is fifth and E last.

questions.stem: Who has the third-highest number of books?
questions.explanation: Most to fewest: C, A, F, D, B, E. C > A > F > D, B has more than only E, so B is fifth and E last.

questions.stem: How many persons have more books than D?
questions.explanation: Most to fewest: C, A, F, D, B, E. C > A > F > D, B has more than only E, so B is fifth and E last. C, A and F have more books than D.

questions.stem: If D has 6 more books than B, which of the following could be the number of F's books?
questions.explanation: Most to fewest: C, A, F, D, B, E. C > A > F > D, B has more than only E, so B is fifth and E last. D has 18 + 6 = 24. F has more than D (24) and fewer than A, who has fewer than C (45). Of the options only 31 lies between 24 and 45.

questions.stem: Who has fewer books than F but more books than B?
questions.explanation: Most to fewest: C, A, F, D, B, E. C > A > F > D, B has more than only E, so B is fifth and E last.

questions.stem: In a certain code, DESK is written as FGUM. How is CHAIR written in that code?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves two places forward: D→F, E→G, S→U, K→M. So C→E, H→J, A→C, I→K, R→T: EJCKT.

questions.stem: If A = 1, B = 2, C = 3 and so on, and CAB is coded as 6 (3 + 1 + 2), what is the code for FACE?
In a certain code language, 'bank gives loan' is written as 'ri su ka', 'loan is cheap' as 'ka nu te' and 'cheap and best' as 'te pa li'. What is the code for 'is'?
questions.explanation: 'Loan' is common to the first two sentences, and so is 'ka'. 'Cheap' is common to the last two, and so is 'te'. The code left for 'is' in 'ka nu te' is 'nu'.

questions.stem: Introducing a man, Sunita said, "He is the father of my husband's only brother." How is the man related to Sunita?
questions.explanation: The father of Sunita's husband's brother is also her husband's father. So the man is Sunita's father-in-law.

questions.stem: M is the mother of N. N is the brother of O. O is the wife of K. How is K related to M?
questions.explanation: O is N's sister, so O is M's daughter. K is O's husband, so K is M's son-in-law.

questions.stem: Asha walks 10 m south, turns left and walks 15 m, turns left again and walks 10 m, then turns right and walks 5 m. How far is she from her starting point, and in which direction?
questions.explanation: Facing south, a left turn faces east (15 m). Another left faces north (10 m), which brings her back level with the start, 15 m east of it. A right turn faces east again: 5 m more makes 20 m east.

questions.stem: A clock is placed flat on a table so that, at 12:00, its minute hand points north. In which direction will the hour hand point at 3:00?
questions.explanation: The 12 on the dial points north, so the 3, a quarter turn clockwise, points east. At 3:00 the hour hand points to the 3: east.

questions.stem: Arun is 17th from the top and 24th from the bottom in his class. How many students are in the class?
questions.explanation: Total = 17 + 24 − 1 = 40. (Arun is counted in both positions, so subtract 1.)

questions.stem: If the English alphabet is written in reverse order, which letter will be 10th from the left?
questions.explanation: In reverse order the 10th letter from the left is the 10th from the end of the normal alphabet: 26 − 10 + 1 = 17th, Q.

questions.stem: Which letter comes next in the series? G, I, L, P, ?
questions.explanation: The gaps grow by one: G (+2) I (+3) L (+4) P (+5) U.

questions.stem: How many pairs of letters in the word GARDEN have as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet?
questions.explanation: G and D have two letters between them in the word (A, R) and in the alphabet (E, F). D and E are next to each other in both. No other pair matches, so there are two.
In every other pair the second number is the square of the first. 8² is 64, not 56.

questions.stem: What is the main advice given in the passage?
options: Avoid every online purchase until the end of the month
Save whatever money is left on the last day of the month
Set aside a fixed part of the salary as soon as it arrives
Borrow money for emergencies instead of keeping savings
Choose a job that pays enough to cover rent and travel
questions.explanation: The passage advises moving 'a fixed part of it into a separate savings account or a recurring deposit before spending anything'. It says saving what is left at month end 'rarely works'.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does saving at the end of the month rarely work?
options: Salaries are paid only at the start of the month
Recurring deposits must be opened on payday
Banks do not accept deposits at month end
Rent rises sharply in the last week of the month
Little or nothing is usually left by then
questions.explanation: The passage says it 'rarely works, because little is ever left'.

questions.stem: Choose the word most similar in meaning to 'cushion' as used in the passage.
questions.explanation: A cushion for emergencies is money kept aside to soften a shock, a safeguard. 'Pillow' is the literal meaning, not the one used here.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

He could not attend the meeting ........ he was unwell.
questions.explanation: Being unwell is the reason he could not attend, so 'because' links the clauses.

questions.stem:
Choose the word that fits the blank to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful.

The cashier counted the notes twice to ........ that none was missing.
questions.explanation: 'Ensure' means make certain. 'Insure' is for insurance and 'assure' takes a person as object ('assure him that').

questions.stem:
Choose the pair of words that fits the two blanks, in order, to make the sentence meaningful.

The festival sale ........ large crowds, and the shops ........ out of stock by evening.
questions.explanation: Large crowds were attracted and the shops ran out of stock. 'Kept out of stock' and 'stayed out of stock' are not the idiom.

questions.stem:
Read the sentence and find the part that contains an error. If there is no error, choose E.

My brother did not (A) / went to the market (B) / yesterday as (C) / it was raining. (D) / No error (E)
questions.explanation: After the auxiliary 'did', the main verb takes its base form: 'did not go', not 'did not went'.

questions.stem:
Which of the following should replace the part in bold to make the sentence correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No improvement'.

The new manager **is having** two cars and a flat in the city.
questions.explanation: 'Have' in the sense of own or possess is a state, not an action, so it is not used in the continuous form: 'The new manager has two cars'.

questions.stem:
The parts of a sentence, labelled P, Q, R and S, are given in jumbled order after the fixed opening. Choose the order that makes a meaningful sentence.

Before leaving the office,

P. and switched off
Q. the clerk locked
R. the lights and fans
S. all the cupboards
questions.explanation: Before leaving the office, (Q) the clerk locked (S) all the cupboards (P) and switched off (R) the lights and fans.

questions.stem: A watch marked ₹3,200 is sold after two successive discounts of 25% and 10%. What is the selling price?
At what rate of simple interest per annum will a sum become three times itself in 20 years?
questions.explanation: Tripling means the interest is twice the sum, 200% in 20 years. 200 ÷ 20 = 10% a year. (5% would only double the sum.)

questions.stem: A salary is increased by 10% and the new salary is then increased by 20%. What is the total increase?
questions.explanation: 1.1 × 1.2 = 1.32, so the final value is 132% of the original: an increase of 32%, not 10 + 20 = 30%.

I. R > U

II. U ≤ S
questions.explanation: I: R > S ≥ T = U gives R > U, true. II: S ≥ T = U gives S ≥ U, which is the same as U ≤ S. Both follow.

I. Some heaters are not fans.

II. Some fans are heaters.
questions.explanation: The heaters that are coolers cannot be fans, so some heaters are not fans (I). Whether any fan is a heater is not settled. Only I follows.

questions.stem:

Statements: Some rods are poles. All poles are beams.

I. All rods are beams.

II. No beam is a rod.
questions.explanation: Only the rods that are poles are known to be beams, so I is not certain. Those rods are beams, so II is false. Neither follows.

questions.stem: Who sits at the left end of the row?
questions.explanation: Left to right: X, Z, V, Y, W. V is 3rd and W 5th, so Y is 4th. Z is 2nd, immediately left of V, and X takes 1st.

questions.stem: Who sits second to the right of Z?
questions.explanation: Left to right: X, Z, V, Y, W. V is 3rd and W 5th, so Y is 4th. Z is 2nd, immediately left of V, and X takes 1st. Z is 2nd; second to the right is 4th, Y.

questions.stem: How many persons sit between X and Y?
questions.explanation: Left to right: X, Z, V, Y, W. V is 3rd and W 5th, so Y is 4th. Z is 2nd, immediately left of V, and X takes 1st. Z and V sit between X (1st) and Y (4th).

questions.stem: If BAT is coded as 2-1-20, how is CUP coded?
questions.explanation: Each letter is replaced by its position in the alphabet: C = 3, U = 21, P = 16.

questions.stem: A's mother is the sister of B, and B is a man. How is B related to A?
questions.explanation: B is the brother of A's mother, which makes him A's maternal uncle.

questions.stem: Rahul walks 16 km west and then 12 km south. What is the shortest distance between him and his starting point?
questions.explanation: The two walks form a right angle, so the distance is √(16² + 12²) = √400 = 20 km. (28 km is the distance walked, not the distance from the start.)
